“No, Victoria, do not thank me,” he answered. His whole soul streamed toward her and he wanted to say more and more; it became confused outbursts, as though he were drunk. “Yes, but Victoria, if you care for me a little ... I do not know, but say you do even if it is not true. Please. Oh, I should promise you to become something, to become great, almost unheard-of. You cannot imagine what I could become; sometimes I brood upon it and know that I am utterly full of deeds not yet done. Often it pours out of me; at night I pace up and down my room because I am full of visions. A man lies in the next room; he cannot sleep and knocks on the wall. At dawn he comes in furious. It does not matter; I pay no heed, for by then I have thought so long about you that I feel you are with me. I go to the window and sing; it begins to grow light, the poplars rustle outside. ‘Good night!’ I say to the day. It is meant for you. ‘Now she is asleep,’ I think, ‘good night, God bless her!’ Then I lie down. So it goes, evening after evening. But I never believed you were as lovely as you are. Now I shall remember you like this when you leave; just as you are now. I shall remember you so clearly ...”

“Are you not coming home?”

“No. I am not finished. Yes, I shall come. I am leaving now. I am not finished, but I shall do all manner of things. Do you ever wander in the garden at home now? Do you ever go out in the evening? I might see you, perhaps be allowed to greet you; not for anything else. But if you care for me a little, if you can bear me, endure me, then say ... Give me that joy ... Do you know, there is a palm that flowers only once in its life, although it grows to seventy years old: the talipot palm. But it flowers only once. I am flowering now. Yes, I shall get money and come home. I shall sell what I have written; I am writing a great book, and I shall sell it now, tomorrow at once, everything I have completed. I shall get a good deal for it. Would you then want me to come home?”

[The source OCR contains the isolated character “a.”]

“Thank you, thank you! Forgive me if I hope too much, believe too much; it is so wonderful to believe an extraordinary amount. This is the happiest day I have lived ...”

He took off his hat and laid it beside him.

Victoria looked about. A lady was coming down the street and, farther up, a woman with a basket. Victoria grew uneasy and reached for her watch.

“Must you go now?” he asked. “Say something before you go; let me hear your ... I love you, and I say it now. It will depend on your answer whether I ... You hold such complete power over me. What do you answer?”

A pause.

He lowers his head. “No, do not say it!” he begged.

“Not here,” she answered. “I shall do it down there.”

They walked on.

“They say you are to marry the little girl, the girl you rescued; what is her name?”

“You mean Camilla?”

“Camilla Seier. They say you are to marry her.”

“Indeed. Why do you ask? She is not grown up. I have been to her home; it is large and rich, a castle like your own. I have been there many times. No, she is not grown up.”

“She is fifteen. I have met her; we have spent time together. I became very fond of her. How lovely she is!”

“I am not going to marry her,” he said.

“Oh, you are not.”

He looked at her. A spasm crossed his face.

“But why do you say this now? Are you trying to direct my attention toward someone else?”

She walked quickly and did not answer. They were outside the chamberlain’s house. She took his hand and pulled him through the gate and up the stairs.

“I am not going in,” he said, half surprised.

She pressed the bell, turned toward him, and her breast rose and fell.

“I love you,” she said. “Do you understand? It is you I love.”

Suddenly she pulled him rapidly down the stairs again, three or four steps, threw her arms around him, and kissed him. She trembled against him.

“It is you I love,” she said.

The entrance door opened above. She tore herself free and hurried up the stairs.
